Benjamin Cowen's framing on NFA Live is the one to carry: Bitcoin sits at the same valuation against the S&P 500 as five to six years ago, while the S&P makes new highs. Per Blockworks, ETF net flows are anemic in both directions and Glassnode has options priced for no move. Miners were the worst asset on the board at minus 6.2 percent, with Cipher and Hut 8 both missing.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, four days early. On July 11 I said Robinhood Chain had to hold $400 million a day of DEX volume by August 10 or the migration was churn. Seven-day volume is near $3 billion, roughly $428 million a day. It cleared.
  • Working. My 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Three independent clocks now point at a low between October and December, and none point up first.
  • Called it, and it cost 13 percent. I said yesterday Galaxy's 830 approved megawatts needed a tenant within days. Novogratz had promised one by the end of summer and did not deliver.
  • Due tomorrow. ERCOT's next Batch Zero round, which the Texas audit suspended.

1. The Coldcard bug was born in 2021, and the coins left this week. Per Swan, a 2021 software integration made Coldcard seed generation fall through to a MicroPython pseudo-random number generator instead of the hardware entropy source it was meant to use. Coinkite puts affected MK2 and MK3 seeds at roughly 40 bits of effective search space, with MK4, MK5 and Q near 72 bits. The design target was 128.

Forty bits is not a lock somebody picked. It is a lock with a thousand keys.

Per the People to follow list, one researcher mapped 4,312 drained addresses with the exact block for each. Per Anthony Pompliano's guests, the total is more than 5,000 people and over $100 million, concentrated among the holders least likely to ever use a custodian. Bitcoin did not move more than about one percent on it.

The position is not a price call. Tilman Holloway expects ETF inflows to tick up three, six and nine months out as burned self-custody holders move to a custodian, against Coinbase and BitGo carrying roughly $5 million of insurance. The remedy circulating on Spaces is generating your own entropy with 100 dice rolls. That tells you how this ends.

The most damning line came from calle on the Crypto list: "not a single vulnerability was found by a US frontier model. Instead, we're spending $10k a day on open weights models like Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 to find vulnerabilities in Bitcoin infrastructure."

2. CLARITY's death is a buy-the-news event, and I am taking the unpopular side. Macro has the vote math tonight: 60 needed, 53 held, cloture filed on a different motion. Here it is a straight disagreement between desks. Per VirtualBacon, Bernstein says failure could trigger the final leg down in crypto valuations and JPMorgan calls it another headwind. Bitwise's Matt Hougan says the SEC and CFTC can supply the same path by rule rather than law. Altcoin Daily puts a failure at Bitcoin "maybe into the 50s, maybe into 48."

James Seyffart's point decides it. Traditional finance treats CLARITY as a catalyst for Bitcoin, not only for alts, so the disappointment is broad rather than confined to tokens that need a legal wrapper.

I am 65/35 that it is already priced. Polymarket went from 50 to 70 percent in January to 15 percent now, and an asset that ignored a $100 million theft is not holding a legislative premium. Hougan is the reason I lean that way. A rulemaking path does not need 60 votes.

3. Galaxy's missing tenant cost it 13 percent, and the frozen queue is why waiting is correct. Per Milk Road, $GLXY fell 13 percent to $19 on a $7.5 billion market cap, and none of it was the numbers. Helios phase one, 200 megawatts leased to CoreWeave for 15 years, is billing toward roughly $80 million a quarter.

Per m0xt on the Stocks list, the pipeline is 5.7 gigawatts with 4.3 contracted, contractable or Batch Zero eligible, and the Texas audit ordered August 3 suspended the next Batch Zero round, due tomorrow. Merlin's first phase is 74 megawatts, one under the 75 megawatt threshold that would have caught it. Caspian at 700 and Selene at 900 are grandfathered.

So the moat held and the announcement did not. I am 60/40 the tenant lands before the audit clears, because a landlord with grandfathered megawatts inside a frozen queue has the only product anyone can plug in.

4. The only live bid in crypto is on Robinhood's chain, and none of it is Bitcoin. Per 0xSammy, Robinhood Chain carries $411 million of DeFi value, $558 million of stablecoins, over $1 billion bridged and nearly $3 billion of seven-day DEX volume, with perpetual futures up 130 percent.

The economics are the interesting part. Apps on the chain took $1.6 million of gross fees in 24 hours and the chain kept $50 thousand. Fat apps, thin chain, no token to dilute. Pons alone runs 64 percent of launchpad volume on a $20 million market cap, and Uniswap has now deployed pools.trade on the same chain to take it.

The other half of the flow is real-world assets, compounding while everything crypto-native shrinks.

On-chainA year agoNow
RWA deposits$2.3 billion$7.4 billion
RWA perpetual notional, July$1.3 billion$150 billion
Tokenized spot volume, monthly$3.4 billion$14 billion

Crypto-native spot DEX volume fell about 70 percent over the same stretch. That is where the money went. Not out of the sector, sideways within it.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $BTC. Roughly 49 percent below October's $126,198 and resting on the 200-week average, with 66.7K the line that matters. Three bottom clocks (Cowen's capitulation event, the 13-month underwater cohort, Altcoin Daily's 200-week analogue) all land in the fourth quarter, none starting with a rally.
  • $GLXY. Down 13 percent for the absence of an announcement rather than a number, while its 830 approved megawatts got scarcer. Tomorrow's suspended Batch Zero round is the next marker.
  • $HOOD. Its chain does $3 billion a week in DEX volume and keeps almost none of the fees. That is deliberate: the chain is the funnel, the brokerage is the business.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins for roughly $105 million, raised $1 billion off the common at about one times net asset value, and spent $1.3 billion retiring converts. Per Apyx's Parker White, the dividend reserve went from six months back to about 18 and nothing puts until September 2027. The deleveraging is working.
  • $COIN. The legislative catalyst is priced at 20 percent for the year and industry volumes fell double digits last quarter. Jack Mallers frames the split honestly: Coinbase cares more about its own chain and alts than about Bitcoin. That is the bull case now, because the chains have the volume.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Warsh opened the door to a September hike, and Trump has been calling him
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.

Yesterday the hawk was a regional president nobody has to obey. Today it is the Chair, and the man who appointed him has been on the phone since May.

Market context. Per the Market list, the Financial Times reports Kevin Warsh is prepared to raise rates in September if inflation prints run hot and markets price in higher borrowing costs. The data underneath him came in firm.

Today's printsReading
Initial jobless claims199,000 against 204,000 expected
Continuing claimsup 24,000 to 1,801,000
Q2 productivity, preliminaryup 1.4 percent against 0.6 expected
Kalshi, a hike at some point this year65 percent

The dollar has not caught up to any of it. MUFG has the dollar index near a seven-week low and still undervalued against eight of the nine other G10 currencies, and Brent came back under $80. Payrolls land tomorrow. CPI on August 12 is the print Warsh named.

The scoreboard.

  • Wrong, and I am reversing it rather than defending it. Yesterday I went 55/45 that September is a hold. The Chair, Governor Lisa Cook and Neel Kashkari all turned hawkish inside 48 hours. I am now 45/55 against a hold.
  • Right, and nearly settled. On Monday I went 85/15 that no CLARITY floor vote happens before the recess. Kalshi prices that at 3 percent.
  • Working, and not the way the tape reads it. My 70/30 on a joint Iran-Oman announcement runs to August 12, and both governments are preparing to designate the strait a transit corridor. Ryan Petersen of Flexport counts one or two transits a day against almost 100 at the peak, at 10 to 15 percent war-risk insurance. The paper is nearly signed and the water is empty.
  • Due tomorrow. Payrolls, which decides whether Warsh's condition is met.

1. Warsh's condition has two legs, and the second one is a mirror. Per the Market list, people close to Warsh say he has acknowledged "early communication mistakes that blurred his message on price stability and Fed reform."

He named two triggers. Hot inflation prints, and markets pricing in higher borrowing costs. The second is the market itself, so a market that prices a hike is helping satisfy the condition for one.

The rest of the committee arrived in the same week. Per the Kalshi list, Governor Lisa Cook said she is ready to raise if inflation stays high and Kashkari said it is "slowly" time to raise. Invesco is the lone dissent that matters, and it argues about whether policy is already restrictive rather than about direction.

Then the part that is not economics. Per the Financial Markets list, the Wall Street Journal reports Trump held multiple undisclosed calls with Warsh, and Bloomberg dates them to May. A Chair turning hawkish while taking private calls from a President who wants cheap money is the least comfortable sequence available, and it argues the hawkishness is real.

2. Treasury needs $739 billion this quarter and the interest line already passed defense. Per ClearValue Tax, the August 3 Treasury statement guides to $739 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing for July through September, meaning debt sold to real buyers rather than shuffled between government accounts. That is $68 billion above the May estimate on less cash flow than projected. October through December is guided at $628 billion, $1.36 trillion across the back half.

The stock and its costFigure
Total debt$39.7 trillion
Interest expense through June$827 billion, against $749 billion a year earlier
Average rate on the debt3.36 percent in FY2025, about 3.42 percent now
Maturing inside twelve months33 percent

That last row is where sections one and two meet. A third of the stock reprices inside a year, so a September hike is not a 2027 problem for the fiscal path. It is a 2026 one. Lyn Alden, on the Stocks list, puts it blunter: for a reserve currency adding $2 trillion a year, the exit is debasement rather than default.

3. Washington is defending the yen with euros, and nobody has seen that before. Per Prof G Markets, the US is intervening in the yen market using euros, and their guest is unambiguous about how unusual that is: "I have never heard of any country intervening in anyone else's market using a third party currency before."

The mechanism is mundane. The US reserve pot is held predominantly in euros and yen, so euros are what there is to sell. The consequence is not. "The US authorities have been in touch with the European Central Bank," and selling euros in size against the yen puts the distortion in a third currency belonging to a central bank that did not ask for any of this.

The failure underneath explains why it got this exotic. Per Trader Mayne, Japan has spent $160 billion this year, including $53 billion and $34 billion on consecutive days last week, and the yen firms for a few days and then goes right back down. His conclusion is that reserves cannot fix it and only rate hikes can. Handle his next step carefully, because he sources it to an AI explainer rather than a report: a forced Bank of Japan hike unwinds the yen carry trade (borrowing cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad), and Japan sells Treasuries into it.

I am not putting odds on that chain. The near end carries enough. Two sources now describe the US financing a foreign currency defense while its own Chair talks about tightening, and MUFG names that intervention as a reason the dollar sits at a seven-week low. The softness is partly a policy choice executed in somebody else's money.

4. CLARITY needs 60 votes, has 53, and nobody filed the paperwork. Per Milk Road, the bill cleared the House 294 to 134 last July and Senate Banking 15 to 9 in May. On the floor it needs 60. Republicans hold 53.

The mechanics killed it before the politics got a turn. Per VirtualBacon, cloture (the motion that ends debate and forces a vote) had to be filed today to ripen in time for a Friday vote, and Majority Leader John Thune filed cloture on a different motion instead. Punchbowl reports Democrats settled on voting no as a bloc unless Republicans move on ethics, illicit finance and stablecoin yield.

The pricing followed the paperwork.

CLARITYNowBefore
Kalshi, passes before recess3 percent20 percent yesterday
Kalshi, becomes law this year20 percent, an all-time low25 percent on Wednesday
Polymarket, becomes law in 202615 to 17 percent50 to 70 percent in January

Friday is the last scheduled working day. Senator Cynthia Lummis says the Senate sits into the weekend with recess starting Monday, the only reason this is not finished already. Per the People to follow list, LuxAlgo answered the countdown with "News flash: It ain't happening."

Here is the calendar that replaces it. The Senate returns September 14 into a handful of working days and a government to fund, against a Fed meeting Warsh has just made live. A committee arguing about a hike does not clear floor time for market-structure legislation, and 20 percent for the whole year says the market has worked that out.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] AMD beat and fell ten percent, and that is the whole market in one print
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bank of America's 7,741 target for the year is done, the S&P closed an entire candle outside its upper Bollinger band for the first time since March 2024, and SpaceX guided to a $100 billion run rate.
item.content:encoded:
Bank of America's 7,741 target for the year is done, the S&P closed an entire candle outside its upper Bollinger band for the first time since March 2024, and SpaceX guided to a $100 billion run rate.

Yesterday I said SpaceX reported into a 34 percent short interest and nobody had a model. It beat and guided to a $100 billion exit run rate. AMD is the more instructive print, because it beat too and got sold ten percent.

Market context. The Hormuz route agreement Macro covers tonight took the last of the war premium out and the tape went vertical. The Nasdaq rose more than 3 percent.

Per Walter Bloomberg on the Market list, Bank of America says the S&P has reached its 2026 target of 7,741, with technicals pointing to 8,000, then 8,234 and potentially 8,541. It sees 7,500 as key support and warns weak August-to-October seasonality, stretched momentum and Friday's payrolls could cap it.

Heisenberg has the stretched part measured. For the first time since March 2024, the entire S&P candlestick body closed outside the upper Bollinger band, by a wide margin. Sunday it was Tesla outside the lower band. Four sessions later the index is outside the upper one.

The scoreboard.

  • Resolved, and it beat. SpaceX reported $7.8 billion of June-quarter revenue against a $6.8 billion expectation and guided to a $100 billion exiting run rate. Per Gene Munster, that implies a December quarter near $22 billion, and December revenue estimates went up about 17 percent.
  • For, after being against. I marked Shay Boloor's Lag-7-becomes-Mag-7 call against on Monday when equal-weight led. A 3 percent Nasdaq day is the other side of that, and the call is live again.
  • Standing. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August runs to August 15 and is not in doubt at a record high.
  • Due tonight. SanDisk reports with an implied move of roughly 15 percent either way.

1. AMD beat, and the market decided that was not enough. Per Con on the Stocks list, AMD produced good numbers and fell about 10 percent after hours having closed the regular session up 7 percent near its highs. It had nearly tripled over the prior year and was up 140 percent year to date going in.

Two things did it. The beat was modest against expectations that were not, and capex rose while free cash flow fell. For a name priced on operating leverage that is the wrong shape regardless of the earnings line.

The read-through is the point. Con concludes AI names now have to beat by a lot rather than merely beat, and he is selling his AI enabler positions on it, naming resistance at $NBIS $220 to $230 and $MU $900, with $AAOI, $NET, $MTSI and $ASYS reporting within days and Nvidia, Marvell and Micron behind them.

The other side is specific and worth holding. Per Shay Boloor on the Market list, Futurum reiterated a Buy with an $800 target, raising its 2027 forecast to $90 billion of revenue and $17.50 of EPS, including $29 billion from server CPUs and $39 billion from data centre GPUs on the Venice ramp, Helios shipments to Meta, Oracle and OpenAI, and up to 14 gigawatts of committed accelerator deployments. That last figure is contracted rather than modelled.

My lean is 60/40 that AMD trades above today's after-hours level in a month. A sell-the-news reaction to a beat in a name up 140 percent is positioning rather than thesis.

2. SpaceX guided to $100 billion and left a $350 billion funding gap. The print was good. The arithmetic behind the guidance is the story.

Per Gene Munster, guidance implies about $8.5 billion of monthly revenue in December, and the Street sits near $100 billion for 2027, up 122 percent. Munster thinks that is low, and at 5 percent month-over-month growth off December he gets $135 billion. His caveat is the honest one: the cloud contracts carry 90-day cancellation provisions, and he waves it away because inference is in the top of the first.

Per SouthernValue on the Stocks list, here is the part nobody guided.

SpaceX capacity and fundingFigure
Data centre capacity todayabout 1.4 GW
End of 2026 target2 GW
2027 targetclose to 10 GW, all Nvidia
Implied capex at $50-60bn per GWroughly $500 billion
Cash on handabout $100 billion
Cash from operations, first half 2026$3 billion
Anthropic and Google spot GPU dealsabout $26 billion of annual recurring revenue
Estimated exit-2026 forward operating cashabout $50 billion
Residual funding gapabout $350 billion

His conclusion is the one to carry: Nvidia customer financing has to come into play. Which puts SpaceX in the same structure as the OpenAI campus, with the chip supplier underwriting the buyer.

3. CXMT refused to cut prices for Apple, and that breaks the bear case on memory. Per Jukan on the Market list, South Korean media reports Apple negotiated with CXMT over mobile DRAM supply prices including LPDDR5X, to ease cost pressure on its next iPhone lineup, and CXMT rejected the request. It insisted on prices higher than or comparable to Samsung and SK Hynix.

If that holds it inverts the story I cut my memory call on. Monday's headline was CXMT doubling capacity past 600,000 wafers a month, and the market read new Chinese supply as a price war. A supposed price-breaker declining to undercut the incumbents on a marquee account is the opposite behaviour, and it says CXMT is optimising for margin rather than share.

The honest caveat is that The AI Investor, relaying the same report, called it "fake news to me, doesn't pass the smell test." He may be right and the sourcing is one media report.

So I am raising the memory call back to 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress, from 55/45 Monday, and doing it on a single-sourced report I have flagged as contested. SanDisk reports tonight into a 15 percent implied move and settles it faster than any of this.

4. The humanoid race got a supply chain this week. Per Wayne Liang on the Market list, four separate national efforts moved at once.

  • Mitsubishi is converting an idle engine plant to build roughly 1,000 humanoids a month
  • Unitree lists in China in a couple of weeks, holding 85 percent of 2025 shipments with more than $20 billion of subsidies behind it
  • Hyundai is targeting a few thousand a year through Boston Dynamics
  • Tesla is ramping Optimus

The tradeable part: downstream flow benefits $CCXI and Agility as the only US-listed pure-play, and he flags plainly that a SPAC merger is higher risk and higher reward.

Converting an engine plant is the detail. The constraint has moved from whether humanoids work to who has idle precision-manufacturing capacity. That is an industrials question, and Japan has more of it than anyone.

5. Gold outran everything and the leadership underneath is not what the index says. Gold rose more than 4 percent to above $4,300, with the tracking fund running from roughly $370 to almost $392 in two sessions. That is a record equity tape and a gold breakout in the same week.

Per AskLivermore on the Stocks list, the dispersion underneath is severe.

Year to dateMove
$SPY+2.59 percent
$QQQ-1.93 percent
$XLK-2.34 percent
$SMH-11.03 percent

Semis down 11 percent while the broad index is up is not a tech-led market, whatever a 3 percent Nasdaq day suggests. His own book is up 5.49 percent, he is staying cautious short term precisely because everyone turned bullish, and his next buys are homebuilders, education providers, micro and small-business enablers, and aging-population REITs. He recently sold Mastercard for a 13 percent gain and added Arm and Marvell.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $AMD. Beat and fell 10 percent after hours on capex up and free cash flow down. Futurum's $800 target rests on 14 gigawatts of committed accelerator deployments, contracted rather than hoped for. This is a positioning reset in a name that had tripled, not a thesis break.
  • $SNDK. Reports tonight with a roughly 15 percent implied move, and it has reacted positively to four of its first five prints since listing. This is the cleanest read on whether commodity DRAM pricing is actually cracking after the CXMT headlines.
  • $SPCX. Beat at $7.8 billion and guided to a $100 billion exit run rate, with the first big lockup opening tomorrow. The funding gap is roughly $350 billion and the answer is probably Nvidia's balance sheet, so own it as a compute business rather than a launch business.
  • $CCXI. The only US-listed pure-play on humanoid components into Mitsubishi at a thousand units a month, Unitree's listing and Optimus ramping. A SPAC structure means size it like the option it is.
  • $GLD. Up four percent above $4,300 while equities printed records and oil fell. If gold is a monetary signal it is the most important chart on the board. If McGlone is right that it is a sock puppet to the S&P, it is beta with better marketing.
  • $XHB. Homebuilders are on AskLivermore's buy list and the cleanest expression of a rate path where six desks disagree. They win on Citi's cut scenario and lose on Kashkari's.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Galaxy lost $85 million and printed the best crypto earnings report of the cycle
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.
item.content:encoded:
The Helios data centre billed its first rent and guided to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins, while Mark Cuban sold most of his Bitcoin because the hedge did not hedge.

Yesterday I said the miners had stopped being a Bitcoin trade. Galaxy Digital proved it with a net loss, a first rent cheque, and guidance that has nothing to do with the price of anything.

Market context. The Nasdaq rose more than 3 percent on the Hormuz route agreement Macro covers tonight. Bitcoin did not lead it, the fourth session running where the equities did the work.

Mike McGlone's line, carried on the Crypto list, is the cleanest statement of the problem: copper, gold and Bitcoin are all sock puppets to the S&P 500 right now. Gold at least got paid for it, up more than 4 percent above $4,300.

Mandelbrot expects knee-jerk movement over the next 24 to 48 hours, thinks it is probably a fakeout with the first move up, and puts his invalidation at 65.8. He has been pounding the table on the Nasdaq proxy over Bitcoin, and a 3 percent index day makes that uncomfortable rather than wrong.

The scoreboard.

  • Working. I moved to 60/40 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. A fourth session of the equity complex ripping without it is the confirmation that call needs.
  • Confirmed the hard way. I have been carrying the Coldcard-drives-money-to-ETFs thread since Monday. Mark Cuban just sold most of his Bitcoin, and the reason was not custody.
  • Due within days. Galaxy's 830 megawatts at Helios needs a tenant, and the Texas queue that everything else depends on is now frozen.

1. Galaxy lost $85 million and the only number that mattered was $18.9 million. Per Milk Road, the headline loss came almost entirely from the Treasury and Corporate segment, which ran $78 million of negative adjusted EBITDA, nearly all of it unrealised markdowns on tokens and investments Galaxy still holds. Crypto fell in the quarter, so the book fell with it. That is beta, not a business.

The business is Helios, an old West Texas mining site converted into an AI data centre campus and leased to CoreWeave for 15 years. In Q2 it started charging rent.

Galaxy data centre segmentQ2
Leasing revenue$18.9 million, the first ever billed
Adjusted gross profit$20.1 million, from $3.1 million in Q1
Adjusted EBITDA$11.5 million, the first positive quarter ever
Phase I critical IT load in serviceall 133 MW
Guided Phase I billing from Q3roughly $80 million per quarter
Project-level adjusted EBITDA marginabove 90 percent

Their analyst wanted Q3 framed near $60 million and got $80 million. A 90 percent margin on contracted rent is a utility, worth a different multiple from anything that mines.

The crypto business held up better than crypto did. Digital Assets adjusted gross profit came in at $66 million, up 34 percent quarter over quarter, while Galaxy's own volumes fell 7 percent and industry volumes fell double digits. Galaxy also signed a multi-year staking agreement with BNY, a custodian overseeing more than $60 trillion.

2. Texas just froze the pipeline, and that makes the approved megawatts more valuable. This is the part with real consequence and almost nobody has priced it.

Galaxy's power pipeline now sits at 5,730 megawatts across Texas after adding three sites. Only 800 megawatts is contracted under an executed lease. The other 4,930 megawatts is identified but uncontracted, and most of it sits behind ERCOT's grid connection queue.

Then, on August 3, Governor Abbott ordered Texas regulators to audit every data centre in that queue before any more advance, with no completion deadline announced. ERCOT paused its Batch Zero study the same day.

The scale of what is stuck: 474 gigawatts of connection requests, against a grid whose record peak demand is roughly 91 gigawatts. Five times the entire peak load of Texas is sitting in a queue that just stopped moving.

That cuts two ways and the second way is the trade. It caps how fast anyone's pipeline can grow, which reprices every announced-but-unconnected megawatt in the state. And it makes the 830 megawatts already approved at Helios scarce in a way it was not last week.

Their analyst goes against his own readers and he is right to. Investors want the next tenant announced immediately. He thinks waiting gets better terms on a 15-year-plus lease, and with the queue frozen, time is on the landlord's side.

The dilution worry is sized. Every phase needs an equity cheque on top of the debt, and working back from Phase II terms he puts the requirement near $1 billion across all three phases against roughly $7 billion of levered free cash flow over the life of the leases, about a 35 percent return on committed equity.

3. Cuban sold because the hedge did not hedge. Per Milk Road on the Stocks list, Mark Cuban has sold the majority of his Bitcoin, and the reasoning is more damaging than the sale.

He bought on one thesis: a better version of gold than gold, a hedge against fiat losing value. Then the test arrived. During the Iran war, geopolitical risk spiked and the dollar slid, and Bitcoin fell while gold went to records. Bitcoin is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar should have pulled global demand in. It did not.

He is reportedly more disappointed in Bitcoin than in Ethereum. Why this matters past one portfolio: the digital-gold framing is the backbone of institutional adoption. It is the reason pension funds, family offices and corporate treasuries started buying at all. If the hedge does not hedge in the one month it was asked to, the next marginal buyer at these prices needs a different reason, and nobody has supplied one.

Set it beside gold up 4 percent above $4,300 this week, and beside Strategy turning seller. The two largest structural arguments for owning Bitcoin, corporate treasury demand and the debasement hedge, both weakened inside five sessions. That is why I am comfortable at 60/40 even with the Nasdaq at a record.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $GLXY. An $85 million loss that is almost entirely paper markdowns, sitting on top of a data centre segment guiding to $80 million a quarter at above 90 percent margins. The three things to watch are whether Q3 leasing actually lands near $80 million, whether a Phase I refinancing appears, and whether the 830 megawatts finds a tenant.
  • $CRWV. The tenant on the other side of Galaxy's 15-year Helios lease, and the counterparty whose credit now underwrites someone else's utility economics. Its own numbers are worse than its landlord's, and that is the whole point of the split.
  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins after four weeks of not buying, and Cuban's exit removes the narrative that made corporate treasuries buyers at all. Watch the premium to net asset value, because it decides whether the coins keep funding the coupon.
  • $IREN. Signed leases rather than hash, and now with the ERCOT queue frozen, already-approved capacity is the scarce asset. The Texas audit is a moat for whoever cleared it and a wall for everyone who did not.
  • $COIN. Macro has the CLARITY window closing with the recess on Saturday and no floor vote scheduled. Nothing today improved that, so the exchange keeps trading on volumes in a quarter when industry volumes fell double digits.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Iran and Oman agreed the Hormuz route, and gold rose four percent anyway
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The strait is being reopened by the mediator nobody named, Kashkari wants a hike immediately, and the Street is now split six ways on September with Kalshi at a coin flip.
item.content:encoded:
The strait is being reopened by the mediator nobody named, Kashkari wants a hike immediately, and the Street is now split six ways on September with Kalshi at a coin flip.

Yesterday Bessent said a Hormuz deal might land today or tomorrow and pointed at Qatari draft text. The deal is landing. The mediator turned out to be Oman, and gold is behaving as though none of it happened.

Market context. Per the Market list, Iran's foreign ministry confirmed three things in the space of two minutes: the geographic characteristics of the route through the Strait of Hormuz have been agreed by Iran and Oman, a joint announcement is in its final stage if "certain third parties" do not interfere, and the agreement "in itself" does not mean the strait is secure.

The rates picture moved further than the geopolitics did.

Where September sitsReading
Kalshi, hold49 percent
Kalshi, 25bp hike47 percent
Kalshi, more than 25bp2 percent
ISM Manufacturing55.6, seventh straight month of expansion
S&P 500 net profit margin16.7 percent, a FactSet record since 2009
Gold futuresup 4 percent on the day, above $4,300

Payrolls land Friday against a 91,000 to 120,000 consensus, and CPI follows on August 12.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and through the wrong door. I went 60/40 yesterday that a Hormuz agreement gets announced inside two weeks. The route is agreed and a joint announcement is in its final stage. I had the channel wrong, because Qatar's draft text was not the one that closed it.
  • Miss, and I am calling it now rather than waiting for the date. On August 2 I went 65/35 that oil would be higher two weeks out. Three sessions later there is a signed route and the risk premium is gone. The call runs to August 16 and it is not coming back.
  • Due Friday. Payrolls, which everything this week routes through.

1. Oman closed it, and the hedge in Iran's own statement is the part to read. The sequence matters because it tells you who actually has leverage. Bessent named Qatar yesterday and put a 24-hour clock on it. What arrived instead was an Iran-Oman route agreement, with Tehran adding two qualifications in the same breath.

The first is procedural: the joint announcement happens if "certain third parties" do not interfere. That is a pre-built escape hatch, and it is aimed at Washington and Jerusalem.

The second is substantive and more important. An agreed route is not a secure strait. Iran is conceding transit geography while explicitly reserving the right to treat passage as conditional. That is the same permissioned-corridor structure it described on Sunday, now with a signature attached.

So the reopening is real and the de-risking is partial. Per the Market list, Russia hit three cargo vessels in the Black Sea the same day. Shipping risk is not a single-theatre story.

I am 70/30 that a joint announcement is made inside a week, up from 60/40 on the route agreement. The 30 is the third-party clause, and the reason I am not higher is that Iran has now written its own permission to walk away into the text.

2. Kashkari wants a hike now, and the Street cannot agree on anything. Per the Market list, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said the Fed should begin raising rates now, backing 25 basis points and warning that delay could force more aggressive tightening if inflation becomes entrenched. He was one of the three who dissented last week.

Then look at how far apart the desks are on the same meeting.

DeskSeptember and beyond
BofA25bp in September, then October and December
JPMorganHold in September, hike in December
GoldmanHold, no more hikes
Morgan StanleyHold through year-end
BarclaysHold through year-end
CitiHold in September, then cuts in October, December and January

BofA's own chief executive Brian Moynihan reiterated the three-hike forecast publicly, saying the labour market is strong while inflation still needs to ease. Citi is at the opposite pole with three cuts. Those cannot both be roughly right.

Janet Yellen supplied the frame that fits the data best. The labour market is functioning well and no longer looks hot enough to fuel inflation, and she is surprised the Middle East conflict and higher oil prices have had such limited economic impact. Her conclusion is that the challenge is still bringing inflation down without harming the economy.

My lean. I am 55/45 that September is a hold, down from the near-certainty of a month ago, and the reason is Kashkari rather than the data. Three dissents plus a regional president publicly campaigning for immediate action is how a committee talks itself into moving. The cleanest read is that the hike is a question of timing, not direction, and Citi's cut scenario requires something to break that has not broken.

3. Goldilocks arrived and the pipeline warning did not clear. Per Milk Road, the case is genuinely strong. ISM at 55.6 is the best since May 2022 and the seventh consecutive month of expansion. S&P 500 net profit margins hit 16.7 percent, the highest FactSet has recorded since it began tracking in 2009. And inflation cooled in the latest reading after several months of increases, partly because easing Iran tensions took energy prices down.

Growth accelerating while inflation falls is the setup that makes everything work, and it is why the equity tape looks the way it does.

Two things sit against it and both are dated. ISM Prices Paid is still at 71.1, elevated on tariff-driven input costs, and that has not passed through yet. And the breadth measure that held the same index at caution yesterday has not recovered.

Which is why Friday matters more than any of it. A payroll print inside consensus puts a labour market under the ISM surge and the Goldilocks read holds. A second consecutive miss near June's 57,000 leaves a strong manufacturing survey next to a weakening jobs market, and that combination has historically resolved toward the jobs data rather than the survey.

4. Gold is up four percent and is not supposed to be. Per the Crypto list, gold futures extended gains to 4 percent on the day and rose above $4,300 an ounce, with the metal running from roughly $370 to almost $392 on the tracking fund in two sessions.

Read that against everything above. The war premium is leaving oil, the strait is reopening, equities are at records and margins are the best since 2009. Gold should have nothing to do.

Instead it is the strongest thing on the board, which says the bid is not geopolitical. It is either the rate path, where a committee arguing about immediate hikes while a Treasury Secretary asks for a Fed facility to be enlarged is exactly the institutional picture gold responds to, or it is currency, with the same Treasury endorsing a stronger yen days after intervening to get one.

Mike McGlone's line is the useful counterweight and it belongs here: copper, gold and Bitcoin are all sock puppets to the S&P 500 right now. If he is right, gold is simply levered risk appetite and carries no signal at all. I lean against him at 60/40, because equities and gold have now risen together for two sessions while oil fell, and that combination is a monetary story rather than a risk-appetite one.

item.title: [Stocks & ETFs] SpaceX reports tonight with 34 percent of its float sold short
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Ninety-five percent of borrowable SpaceX stock is already out on loan, the first $100 billion lockup opens Thursday, and Caterpillar just cleared $20 billion of quarterly sales for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
Ninety-five percent of borrowable SpaceX stock is already out on loan, the first $100 billion lockup opens Thursday, and Caterpillar just cleared $20 billion of quarterly sales for the first time.

Yesterday SpaceX printed an all-time low the session before its first earnings report. Today it bounced into the print, and the borrow data says almost everyone has already picked a side.

Market context. The oil move Macro covers this evening did the work here. Futures hit a record high on Bessent's Hormuz comments, and the index arrives at the level that has capped it since spring.

Per Scott Redler on the Financial Markets list, the S&P cleared the 7448 line and pushed to 7610 in the prior session, and the index "may be trying to leave its 10-plus week range." He wants it to hold above 7448, with 7620 the bigger level overhead. Frank Cappelleri's 7,680 target from late April is still live per Ryan Detrick, and Societe Generale now carries 8,000 on broadening earnings strength.

Leadership is the part that does not fit the record. The equal-weight S&P keeps outrunning the cap-weighted index and the rotation is carrying into August. That is not what a megacap-led tape looks like. Tonight's SpaceX and AMD prints land in tomorrow's edition.

The scoreboard.

  • Against, on day one. I carried Shay Boloor's call yesterday that the Lag 7 turn back into the Mag 7 and the generals lead again. The equal-weight index outrunning the cap-weighted one is the opposite of that, and the rotation is where the money actually went.
  • Standing, and improving. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August is intact with futures at a record. The call runs to August 15.
  • Due tonight. AMD reports, and SpaceX reports for the first time in company history.
  • Due Thursday. The first SpaceX lockup, more than $100 billion of stock, begins unlocking two days after the print.

1. The SpaceX print is the most crowded short in the market. Per zerohedge on the Financial Markets list, S3 data shows 95 percent of SpaceX stock available to borrow is out on loan, and short interest is 34 percent of the float. The stock hit an all-time low near $104 yesterday and traded back to $118 before the open.

Per Kyle Reidhead on the Crypto list, here is what the print actually turns on.

LineWhere it stands
Expected revenue$6.8 billion
Expected cash burn$10.9 billion
Starlink ARPU$99 in 2023, $66 last quarter, street wants $65.50
AI capex last quarter$7.7 billion, 76 percent of all company spending
Anthropic compute deal$1.25 billion a month through 2029
2026 X revenue, consensusabout $2.9 billion
Consensus EPSa $1.26 loss to a $0.33 profit

That last row is the tell. When the sell side's range spans a loss and a profit, nobody has a model, and a 34 percent short interest into a no-model print is a squeeze setup rather than a thesis.

Heisenberg's framing is the honest one and it is worth quoting: it is so obvious the stock goes down tomorrow that it becomes obvious not to short it, because everyone thinks it is obvious. My lean is 55/45 that SpaceX trades higher on Thursday than it closes tonight, and the reason is mechanical rather than fundamental. The lockup is the real event, and a squeeze into a supply cliff is how the worst entries get made.

2. Caterpillar cleared $20 billion in a quarter for the first time, and the reason is data centres. Per the Financial Markets list, Caterpillar surged as quarterly sales topped $20 billion for the first time in company history, driven by the AI data centre build. Heisenberg's read was two words and a question mark: the AI boom is just getting started.

This is the cleanest version of a trade that keeps being mispriced. Everyone argues about whether the hyperscalers earn a return on $860 billion of capex. Caterpillar does not need them to. It sells the generators, the earthmoving and the power equipment into the build, books the revenue on delivery, and carries none of the residual-value risk that makes the neocloud arithmetic fail.

The same logic ran through Vertiv, which raised full-year guidance across the board and still fell double digits, and it is why the picks-and-shovels layer keeps being the least crowded way to own the theme.

3. Memory is being repriced on supply for the second session running. Yesterday Reuters had CXMT weighing a second Beijing fab that would take its capacity past 600,000 wafers a month, and I cut my memory call to 55/45 on it. Today the complex is still working out what that means.

Per the Financial Markets list, Marvell is soaring, and Scott Redler had Nvidia, Micron, SpaceX and SanDisk as the four names on his premarket board. The distinction that matters has not changed since Kyle Reidhead drew it: CXMT's new capacity is commodity DRAM, and high-bandwidth memory is sold out through 2026.

So the right way to hold this is that a China supply headline hits the commodity end and the margin structure, while the AI-critical end stays contracted. I am staying 55/45 that memory multiples expand before they compress, unchanged, because nothing today touched the HBM book. SanDisk reports tomorrow and is the better read on where commodity pricing actually is.

4. The Hormuz war trades are unwinding before the war ends. There is a whole trade built on the closure, and it has spent two sessions going the wrong way. The names are Frontline in tankers, RTX in defence and ExxonMobil in energy, and each one was priced off a strait that stays shut and shipping that stays rerouted.

Bessent's draft-text comment takes the top off all three at once. Brent at $81.50 after a 4.7 percent Monday fall is not a war premium, it is the market pricing a signature.

The asymmetry now runs the other way. If a deal lands this week these names give back the rest of the move, and if Iran denies it for a fourth time they gap back. Anas Alhajji's open question decides the medium term: can Saudi Arabia actually reroute 6 million barrels a day through the northern Red Sea? Nobody has answered it, and until somebody does the tanker trade has a floor under it that the defence names do not.

5. Apple is down five straight and starting to trade like a defensive. Per Heisenberg on the Financial Markets list, Apple is holding $300 after five down days and a peak-to-trough fall of more than 13 percent, and it has been inversely tracking the Nasdaq proxy.

His setup is the interesting part rather than the level. Once the Nasdaq takes a breather after a large five-day run, he expects defensive money to rotate back into Apple for a bounce. That is a rotation argument dressed as a chart, and it fits the breadth data better than the megacap-leadership story does.

The overhang is real and it is not priced out. Apple guided September below consensus and blamed the memory shortage explicitly, and Bloomberg has MacBook Air orders slipping to September on the same crunch. A component squeeze that delays the best-supplied hardware company in the world does not clear because the stock got cheap.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Reports tonight into 34 percent short interest with 95 percent of the borrow already lent, then more than $100 billion of stock starts unlocking Thursday. The print and the supply cliff are 48 hours apart, so anything you do here is a position on the sequencing rather than on the business.
  • $CAT. First $20 billion quarter in company history on data centre demand, and it carries no residual-value risk on the GPUs. The cleanest non-AI way to own the AI build, and the one nobody argues about at dinner.
  • $AAPL. Holding $300 after five down days and 13 percent off the high, inversely tracking the Nasdaq. A defensive bounce candidate with a real memory-cost overhang into September, so size it as a trade and not a thesis.
  • $FRO. The tanker leg of the Hormuz trade, and the one with a floor under it, because rerouting 6 million barrels a day through the Red Sea is unsolved even if the strait reopens. Rates stay elevated on distance travelled rather than on risk.
  • $SNDK. Reports tomorrow and is the honest read on commodity DRAM pricing after the CXMT capacity headline. High-bandwidth memory is sold out through 2026, so this print tells you about the other end of the market and not about the AI book.
  • $VRT. Raised full-year guidance across the board and fell double digits anyway. Either the market knows something about power-equipment margins or that is the kind of reaction that reverses.

item.title: [Bitcoin & Crypto] Strategy became a seller and Bitcoin sat out the best macro day in weeks
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.
item.content:encoded:
Miners rallied 9.6 percent on data centre leases while Bitcoin finished flat against a Nasdaq up 1.4 percent, and the most reliable structural bid in the market spent last week selling.

Yesterday Michael Saylor sold $102 million of Bitcoin and Jim Cramer capitulated on quantum risk. Today the tape showed what that costs: a record-high equity session, a Hormuz de-escalation, and Bitcoin did not move at all.

Market context. Per 0xResearch, Monday split the complex clean down the middle. Bitcoin was flat at negative 0.02 percent while the Nasdaq gained 1.4 percent and the S&P added 1.2.

The equities did all the work.

SectorMove
Crypto Miners+9.6 percent
Crypto Equities+4.5 percent
Modular+2.8 percent
DEXs-5.7 percent
Solana Eco-3.3 percent
Launchpad-2.9 percent

Token performance was fragmented rather than themed. The macro backdrop that lifted everything else, the yen intervention and the Iran de-escalation, is Macro's story tonight. What it did here was give crypto equities a bid and leave the tokens alone.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and it is early. I went 55/45 yesterday that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000. Flat on a day the Nasdaq rose 1.4 percent is the weak-tape confirmation that call needs, though nothing is settled.
  • Corroborated by two more names. I carried Anthony Pompliano's read that the Coldcard hack pushes money toward ETFs and third-party custody. Eric Balchunas and Dave Weisberger both landed independently in the same place today.
  • Resolved, and it is the one that matters. Strategy stopped being a buyer. After four weeks without a purchase it sold 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks.

1. The most reliable buyer in the market is now a seller, and that is a structural change. Per 0xResearch, Strategy disclosed selling 1,638 Bitcoin last week to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks. That follows four straight weeks with no purchase at all.

Read it as plumbing rather than sentiment. For five years Strategy was a price-insensitive buyer that absorbed supply on every drawdown, and the market got used to that floor. It has now inverted, losing its most dependable structural buyer and gaining a seller with a dividend obligation. That is forced flow, and it does not care about your levels.

The mechanism does not reverse quickly. The preferred stack is serviced in dollars, so if the equity cannot be issued above net asset value, the coins fund the coupon. That treadmill speeds up as the discount widens.

I am moving to 60/40 that Bitcoin sees $58,000 before $75,000, up from 55/45 yesterday. The upgrade is not about the macro, which improved today. It is that the bid I was implicitly relying on has been withdrawn and replaced by supply.

2. The miners are no longer a Bitcoin trade, and this week proved it. Twelve of the thirteen constituents are higher over the past week, and the leaders are not subtle.

MinerOne-week move
CIFR+24.9 percent
IREN+20.8 percent
HUT+19.3 percent

The driver is contracts rather than hash price. Per 0xResearch, IREN's $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals and Hut 8's second $9.8 billion lease are still working through the sector. And per the Financial Markets list, Bitdeer jumped 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing data centre lease.

Sixteen years is the number to sit with. That is a utility contract rather than a mining business, and it reprices the equity off a different curve entirely. A miner with a signed decade-plus lease is a landlord.

So the sector has quietly split. The names converting substations into AI capacity trade on lease duration and counterparty credit. The ones still selling hash trade on Bitcoin, which went nowhere today. Own the first group and stop calling it a Bitcoin proxy.

3. The Coldcard hack is turning into an ETF marketing campaign, and the argument is uncomfortable because it is right. Per the Crypto list, Eric Balchunas put it most sharply: the hack could spur greater migration to ETFs, because "what used to be seen as a bug by coiners, dorky boomer TradFi, may all of a sudden seem like a feature, large established financial institutions with decades of experience safeguarding client assets, especially versus a Canadian company with five employees."

Dave Weisberger landed there separately, calling it a gift to ETFs and custodians. Three named voices in two days, including one who covers nothing but funds. Set it against the scale: more than $100 million gone from over 5,000 wallets, in an attack Bloomberg still calls ongoing, caused by a flaw in Coinkite's random number generator rather than anything in Bitcoin.

The uncomfortable part is that the people hit were the ones who followed the instructions. Self-custody is the ideological core and the failure was a vendor's code, not user error. If the resolution is that ordinary holders route through BlackRock, the asset wins on price and loses the argument it was built on.

4. The institutional plumbing kept building while the price did nothing. Three items landed today that have nothing to do with the tape and everything to do with the next cycle.

Wells Fargo is rolling out tokenized deposits for enterprises and corporates, with 24/7 onchain access to working capital. A money-centre bank issuing them is the tokenization thesis arriving through the front door.

Polymarket is seeking investment at more than a $20 billion valuation, per zerohedge, and separately picked up exclusive US streaming rights to Serie A. A prediction market buying live sports rights is a distribution play, and it says where the venue thinks its next users come from.

And per 0xResearch, MetaDAO's decision markets passed a real stress test. An attacker filed UMBRA-004 on July 31 seeking to move $1.57 million of USDC, effectively Umbra's entire treasury, to their own wallet. Umbra governs through conditional PASS and FAIL markets rather than token voting, and a proposal executes only if PASS holds a higher time-weighted price, so the market priced the theft as bad and it failed. Governance attacks beat token voting when an attacker can rent enough votes. Pricing the outcome instead of counting them made this one unprofitable.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MSTR. Sold 1,638 coins last week and has not bought in five. The preferred dividends and STRC buybacks have to be funded, and if the equity will not print at a premium to net asset value, the stack keeps paying for the coupon. Watch the premium, not the Bitcoin price.
  • $IREN. Up 20.8 percent on the week on $2.8 billion of AI-cloud deals. The thesis is now lease duration and counterparty credit, so the right comparison is a data centre operator rather than a miner.
  • $BTDR. Up 23 percent on a 16-year AI and high-performance-computing lease. Sixteen years of contracted revenue is the longest visibility anyone in this sector has, and the market repriced it in a session.
  • $COIN. Macro has CLARITY at 27 percent for the year with no floor vote scheduled and the recess on Saturday. The near-term catalyst is gone, so what is left is the exchange business and the agentic payment rails, which still carry no revenue line.
  • $HOOD. The other side of the same regulatory coin, with event contracts already out-earning both its equities and crypto lines. Less exposed to a CLARITY failure than Coinbase and more exposed to prediction markets, where Polymarket's $20 billion raise sets the comparison.

item.title: [Macro & Policy] Bessent says a Hormuz deal may land tomorrow, and oil gave up two percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Qatar has draft text ready, futures hit a record high on the headline, and the same Treasury Secretary spent the morning telling the Federal Reserve to upsize one of its own facilities.
item.content:encoded:
Qatar has draft text ready, futures hit a record high on the headline, and the same Treasury Secretary spent the morning telling the Federal Reserve to upsize one of its own facilities.

Three days ago Iran was denying it had agreed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while CENTCOM redirected 35 vessels around it. This morning the Treasury Secretary said a deal might be signed by tomorrow. Everything else on the board moved off that one sentence.

Market context. Per the Financial Markets list, Scott Bessent said "I think there's a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait," and Qatar has already prepared draft text for an agreement. Futures hit a record high on it. Oil rose 2 percent and then fell 2 percent inside the same session, with Brent for October at $81.50.

The domestic data was the quiet half and it was strong.

PrintReading
July ISM Manufacturing55.6 percent, best since May 2022
ISM Prices Paid71.1, still elevated on tariff-driven input costs
Atlanta Fed GDPNow, Q3raised from 5.0 to 6.2 percent
US trade balancenegative $73.3 billion against negative $73.0 expected, prior negative $77.6

Ahead: payrolls Friday August 7, consensus 91,000 to 120,000 after June's 57,000 miss, then CPI on August 12.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and it was mine to publish. I said yesterday the Camp David notepad reading "buy Japanese yen $5-10 bil" was deliberate rather than accidental. Confirmed from both sides. The New York Fed, acting for Treasury, sold euros to buy yen on Friday, both governments acknowledged it Monday, and USD/JPY fell from above 163 to around 156.
  • Against, for a second day. I went 65/35 on August 2 that oil would be higher two weeks out. Bessent is now negotiating the exact opposite. That call is losing and I am not going to dress it up.
  • Confirmed and dated. The CLARITY Act cleared the House and Senate Banking, sits on the legislative calendar, and still has no scheduled vote with the recess on Saturday.

1. The strait is being traded before it is open, and the draft text is the tell. Per the Financial Markets list, Anas Alhajji timed the tape precisely: oil rose 2 percent, then fell 2 percent once Bessent spoke. Per 0xResearch, Trump's decision to postpone further strikes against Iran had already sent Brent down 4.7 percent on Monday.

So the risk premium has come out in two steps on two statements, and neither of them is an open waterway. Qatar having draft text is the genuinely new fact, because a mediator does not circulate paper without a landing zone in view.

The cost of the closure is now measurable in fiscal terms. Alhajji counts EU governments committing roughly 12 to 16 billion euros in subsidies and measures to cushion the crisis and hold energy costs down. In most countries that spending prevented a recession, growth stayed very low anyway, and the borrowing still has to be repaid.

My lean, and it is a downgrade from Sunday. I am 60/40 that a Hormuz agreement is announced inside two weeks, up from roughly even, because Qatari draft text plus a US Treasury Secretary putting a date on it is a different state from either side making claims. The 40 is that Iran has denied three separate reopening reports in four days.

2. The Treasury Secretary spent the morning directing a Federal Reserve facility. This is the item almost nobody priced. Per the Crypto list, Bessent's statement on the yen ran past the intervention itself and into instrument design.

His words. "We will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention. The FIMA Repo Facility is an important backstop. We would encourage it to be upsized in the coming months."

Jeff Park caught what that means and said it in one line: "FIMA is entirely a Fed tool, not a Treasury tool. Welcome to the Bessent-Warsh era of Fed interdependence."

He is right and it matters more than the yen level. The Foreign and International Monetary Authorities repo facility lets foreign central banks borrow dollars against their Treasury holdings rather than dumping them. It is the Fed's plumbing for stopping a forced sale of US paper. A Treasury Secretary publicly asking for it to be enlarged is fiscal authority making a monetary request in the open, and neither institution corrected the other.

Bessent also went further than a stabilisation argument, saying Treasury "strongly supports Japan's decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen," and describing the Takaichi government as moving into a new phase of Abenomics. That is the United States endorsing a stronger yen, which tightens the cheapest funding pipe in global markets.

3. The economy printed strong and the index that watches it still says caution. Per Milk Road, July ISM at 55.6 percent answered the growth question in the clearest way available, GDPNow extended to 6.2 percent rather than retracing, and the stress score fell to its floor while the macro buffer sat at full strength. Oil held below $80, copper rose, freight costs fell and the curve steepened.

And their posture stayed at caution at 75 percent exposure, for one reason. Breadth on the market side fell 0.46 on the week to 0.18, working directly against every other gain, even as the equal-weight S&P keeps outrunning the cap-weighted index and the rotation carries into August. The rotation is visible in prices and absent from the breadth score, and that gap is the only thing between here and a full risk-on posture.

Their three conditions to clear it are worth writing down: breadth stops falling, Friday's payrolls confirm a labour market under the ISM surge, and the August 12 CPI leaves six-month core flat. That last one is the live risk, because ISM Prices Paid at 71.1 is a tariff-driven pipeline warning that has not bled through yet.

Mohamed El-Erian adds the distributional caveat on the Financial Markets list: more than 80 percent of reporters have beaten expectations, and releases like McDonald's this morning keep showing the K, with pressure concentrated on lower-income households.

4. CLARITY has four days and no floor time. Per Arbitrage Andy, the bill has cleared the House and advanced through Senate Banking, and it is formally on the Senate legislative calendar, meaning it is eligible for a floor vote. It has no scheduled vote and Congress leaves for recess on Saturday.

The arithmetic is the whole story. Cloture needs 60 votes, so roughly seven Democratic senators have to cross. Some backed earlier committee versions and negotiations have since stalled on three things: ethics provisions covering government officials' own crypto activity, consumer protection language, and stablecoin-related banking concerns.

Polymarket prices 27 percent that it is signed into law this year. That is the number to carry, and it is down from 82 percent in February.

The consequence if it lapses is not a price move, it is a jurisdictional vacuum. Without the bill the SEC and CFTC turf war stays unresolved and exchanges, token issuers and crypto businesses keep operating in legal limbo. I am 85/15 that no floor vote happens before the recess, and the more interesting question is whether September brings a rewrite or a shelving.
